section.title: Not to Us, but to Your Name
section.sectionRationale: This third Hallel psalm refuses every claim to human glory, redirecting all praise to God alone while contrasting the living, active LORD with the mute, powerless idols of the nations, then closing with a call for the living to bless the LORD forever.
section.thesis: All glory belongs to God alone, never to His people, because He is a living God who acts as He pleases, unlike the lifeless idols that can neither speak, see, nor save, and so trusting Him alone is the only fitting response of the living.
section.frameNote: Five movements: glory refused for self and given to God alone, verses 1-3; idols exposed as powerless and lifeless, verses 4-8; a threefold call to trust the LORD as help and shield, verses 9-11; the promise of His blessing on small and great alike, verses 12-15; and the closing call for the living to praise Him forever, verses 16-18.

units.label: Not to us, but to Your name
units.note: glory refused for self, given to God alone

verses.text: Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory, because of Your loving devotion, because of Your faithfulness.
Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?"
Our God is in heaven; He does as He pleases.

units.label: Their idols are silver and gold
units.note: mute, powerless, made by human hands

verses.text: Their {{elilim|idols}} are silver and gold, made by the hands of men.
They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see;
they have ears, but cannot hear; they have noses, but cannot smell;
they have hands, but cannot feel; they have feet, but cannot walk; they cannot even clear their throats.
Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them.

units.label: O Israel, trust in the LORD

verses.text: O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield.
O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield.
You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield.
The LORD is mindful of us; He will bless us. He will bless the house of Israel; He will bless the house of Aaron;
He will bless those who fear the LORD, small and great alike.
May the LORD give you increase, both you and your children.
May you be blessed by the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.

units.label: It is we who will bless the LORD

verses.text: The highest heavens belong to the LORD, but the earth He has given to mankind.
It is not the dead who praise the LORD, nor any who descend into silence.
But it is we who will bless the LORD, both now and forevermore. Hallelujah!

elilim.gloss: Idols, worthless things, a term related to a root meaning nothingness. The word itself mocks the objects it names, calling attention to their impotence in stark contrast to the living, acting God of verse 3.

basic.context: This psalm refuses to let Israel's people receive credit for God's own faithfulness, redirecting all glory to His name, then satirizes the lifeless idols of the surrounding nations before calling every group in Israel, priests and people alike, to trust the LORD who alone is a living help and shield.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's structure, from refusing self-glory to exposing idols to calling for trust to promising blessing to demanding living praise, models a worship that is entirely God-centered, rooted in His character rather than in human achievement or manufactured religion.
basic.originalLanguages: The idols are called elilim, worthless things, a term whose very sound in Hebrew mocks their pretension to power, verse 4. Unlike them, the LORD does as He pleases, verse 3, acting freely and sovereignly rather than remaining inert like silver and gold shaped by human hands.
basic.typology: The psalm's insistence that only the living can praise the LORD, verse 17, anticipates the fuller resurrection hope of the New Testament, and its warning that idolaters become like their idols, verse 8, anticipates Paul's teaching that people are transformed into the image of whatever they worship, whether idols or the living Christ, 2 Corinthians 3:18.
basic.christ: This psalm's refusal to glorify anyone but God, not to us, but to Your name be the glory, verse 1, anticipates Christ's own perfect self-emptying obedience that results in the Father highly exalting Him, Philippians 2:9-11, so that every knee bows to the name above every name. The psalm's contrast between lifeless idols and the living God who does as He pleases is fulfilled in Christ, the image of the invisible God, Colossians 1:15, who alone gives true sight, hearing, and life to those who trust Him.
basic.god: God alone deserves glory, acting in sovereign freedom, unlike the mute and powerless idols fashioned by human hands. He is mindful of His people, promising blessing to small and great alike, and He is the Maker of heaven and earth, worthy of the praise only the living can offer Him.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 44:9-20 similarly exposes the folly of crafting and trusting idols made by human hands. Acts 17:29 echoes this psalm's logic in Paul's sermon to the Athenians. Philippians 2:9-11 shows the pattern of glory refused for self and given wholly to God fulfilled in Christ's exaltation.
basic.oneStory: All glory belongs to the living God alone, never to lifeless idols or to human achievement, a pattern of self-emptying glory-giving fulfilled perfectly in Christ, who refused to grasp at glory for Himself yet was exalted by the Father to the name above every name, so that the truly living, in Him, forever bless the LORD.

context.literary:
The psalm moves like a liturgy with changes of voice, and it is easier to read as a conversation than as a single speaker. Verses 1 to 3 are a congregation's prayer, in the first person plural, with a question from the nations and a confession in answer. Verses 4 to 8 step back into a cool, almost teasing description of other people's gods. Verses 9 to 11 are a leader's summons, three times repeated, and each summons is followed by the same line, 'He is their help and shield,' which shifts to the third person and sounds like the people or priests answering back. Verses 12 to 15 are a blessing spoken over the worshippers, and verses 16 to 18 return to the first person plural with a resolve to praise.

A repeated verb ties these parts together. Verse 3 says the Lord does all that pleases Him, verse 4 calls the idols the work of human hands, verse 8 speaks of those who make them, and verse 15 names the Lord as Maker of heaven and earth. Those words for doing, work, making and maker are all one family in Hebrew, so the passage is set up as a contest between a God who acts and gods who are acted upon.

A second thread is trust and blessing. 'Those who trust in them' in verse 8 shares its verb with the three calls to 'trust in the LORD' in verses 9 to 11. Verses 12 to 15 then run on 'bless' as the Lord's action toward His people, and verse 18 closes the circle by making 'bless' the people's action toward Him. The Lord blesses us, and we bless the Lord.

The listing of body parts in verses 5 to 7 is also constructed. Mouth, eyes, ears, nose, hands, feet and throat make seven, each paired with a failure. The number is probably deliberate, a complete inventory of everything a living god would need, and each is found missing.
context.historical:
The psalm contains no name or date, and its situation can only be inferred. The taunt in verse 2, 'Where is their God?', is the sneer that defeated peoples heard in the ancient world, and it appears in Psalm 79:10 and Joel 2:17 as an argument in prayer. The psalm may come from a time when Israel was humiliated and needed to hear that its God did not lose face with its fortunes. It is just as likely that it was written for the temple worship generally, since the three groups called to trust in verses 9 to 11 are the standing parts of the assembly.

The idol passage reflects the way images were understood in the ancient Near East. A statue was made by craftsmen from precious metal and wood, and in Mesopotamia texts describe rituals for opening the mouth of a new image so that it could be treated as alive, after which it was fed, clothed and carried in procession. Isaiah mocks this routine in Isaiah 40:19-20, 44:9-20 and 46:1-2, where the gods are loads on animals' backs. Jeremiah 10:3-5 ridicules the statue that must be carried because it cannot walk. Psalm 115 was therefore drawn from a world in which images had a recognised place in worship, and its mockery cut against the grain.

The 'house of Aaron' is the priesthood, and the call to trust the Lord comes with a certain irony. It was Aaron who fashioned the gold calf at Sinai, Exodus 32:2-4. The priests of Israel are being addressed as the heirs of that failure.

'Those who fear the LORD' in verse 11 shows up in similar lists in Psalm 118:2-4 and Psalm 135:19-20. It was a way of naming everyone who revered the Lord, including those who might have been outside the birth families of Israel and Aaron.
context.canonical:
Verses 4 to 8 are nearly repeated in Psalm 135:15-18, where the Hallelujah psalm ends with the same silent idols and the same line that those who make them become like them. The close agreement suggests a shared liturgical tradition, and the small differences are telling: Psalm 115 says the idols cannot clear their throats, while Psalm 135 says there is no breath in their mouths. The same mockery runs through the prophets. Isaiah 44:9-20 follows a carpenter who burns half a tree to cook his meal and bows to the other half, Habakkuk 2:18-19 calls the idol a teacher of lies, and Jeremiah 10:3-5 compares idols to scarecrows.

Verse 1 echoes a line of prophetic theology about the Lord's name. Ezekiel 36:22-23 says the Lord will act not for Israel's sake but for His holy name, which was profaned among the nations, and Isaiah 48:11 says He will not yield His glory to another. Psalm 115 prays from inside that logic. The taunt of verse 2 recalls Moses pleading in Numbers 14:13-16 that the Egyptians would hear of it.

The living and the dead of verse 17 belong to a cluster of psalms and prayers about the silence of Sheol, Psalm 6:5, Psalm 30:9, Psalm 88:10-12 and Isaiah 38:18-19, where the living can thank God and the dead cannot. The same psalms also contain the first signs of hope that God will not abandon His own to the grave, Psalm 16:10 and Psalm 49:15.

Paul and the New Testament take up the idol critique, 1 Corinthians 8:4-6, Acts 14:15 and 1 Thessalonians 1:9, and the pattern of becoming like what we revere appears in Romans 1:23 and 2 Corinthians 3:18. The final 'small and great' of verse 13 returns in Revelation 19:5, in the great Hallelujah chorus.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted God's people to handle humiliation without losing their nerve. When the nations ask where Israel's God is, the temptation is to defend the people's honour or to retreat into private belief. The psalm instead opens by refusing credit and asking God to protect His own name, and it puts the weight on His character, 'loving devotion' and 'faithfulness.' The people ask for vindication on the ground of who He is, not on the ground of who they are.

He also meant to give his hearers a settled answer to the sneer. The reply is not an argument from evidence but a comparison between two kinds of gods. The one in heaven acts, and the ones on the shelf cannot so much as clear their throats. The humour is deliberate: ridicule is a way of showing that something is not a serious competitor.

The central warning of verse 8 is that worship shapes the worshipper. Whatever one gives oneself to, one starts to resemble, so the idolater's real danger is not only a mistaken belief about divine things but a slow loss of life. In the same way, those who trust the living Lord are meant to become living and responsive, which is why the psalm ends with praise and not with a lecture.

Finally he meant the three groups of verses 9 to 11 and the matching blessings of verses 12 and 13 to be spoken aloud in turn, so that every part of the assembly hears its own name called and its own promise given.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes idols as silver and gold, and it prescribes trust in the Lord, praise by the living and glory given to Him alone. It does not command ridicule of people. The target is the object of worship and the cost to those who worship it, and a reader who turns verses 4 to 8 into contempt for neighbours has stepped outside what the psalm does.

Verses 12 to 15 describe a blessing that includes 'increase, both you and your children.' It should be read as a covenant blessing sung over a worshipping community, not as a promise that every faithful family will grow in number or wealth. The same Psalter includes laments from faithful people who lost children and land. What the verses do secure is the character of the God who is 'mindful' of His people and who blesses small and great alike, with no ranking of importance.

Verse 17 describes the experience of the dead from the standpoint of public worship, in the language the old covenant used. It is not an instruction to treat death as the end or a comment on what the dead experience, and the New Testament speaks to that more clearly. The application today is not to be anxious about idols made of silver but to ask what shapes us. Modern forms of the same problem, such as money, image or power, have the same effect on those who give themselves to them, and the psalm's remedy is the same: give the glory to God and trust Him as help and shield.

debates.question: Who are 'those who fear the LORD' in verses 11 and 13?

views.label: All faithful Israelites, grouped with the other two
views.case: Verses 9 to 11 name three circles, Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD, and Psalm 118:2-4 follows the same pattern. Some take the third group as a way of describing the pious laity who stand alongside the whole nation and its priests, so that the list moves from the nation to the clergy and back to every believer.

views.label: Gentile God-fearers who attached themselves to Israel
views.case: Because the third group is set apart from Israel and Aaron, others see in it proselytes and sympathisers outside the bloodline. Psalm 135:19-20 adds 'house of Levi' and then the same phrase. On this view the psalm already makes room for outsiders under the same help and shield.

views.label: A summary term that includes everyone before it
views.case: A third view treats the phrase as an umbrella for all who honour the Lord, with Israel and Aaron as the leading examples. The words 'small and great alike' in verse 13 then stretch it across every rank.

debates.bearing: The difference matters for how widely the invitation reaches. Even on the narrowest reading, trust is demanded of priest and layperson alike, and on the widest the promise reaches anyone who reveres the Lord. Either way, no hearer is excused.

debates.question: Does verse 17 deny any life with God after death?

views.label: It reflects the limited hope of the Old Testament era
views.case: Passages like Psalm 6:5, Psalm 88:10-12 and Isaiah 38:18-19 speak of Sheol as a place of silence where praise ceases. On this reading the poet simply held the view that the realm of the dead was cut off from active worship, and later revelation brought what earlier saints only glimpsed.

views.label: It speaks only about public praise in the land of the living
views.case: The verse says the dead do not praise and then promises 'we will bless the LORD,' meaning the worshipping community, now and for ever. It contrasts those who can still join the assembly with those who cannot, without saying whether the dead exist with God.

views.label: It stands beside genuine early hopes of resurrection
views.case: Other psalms reach for more. Psalm 16:10 hopes that God will not abandon the soul to Sheol, Psalm 49:15 says God will take me to Himself, and Psalm 73:24 expects to be received in glory. Jesus used the claim that God is God of the living to argue for resurrection, Matthew 22:32.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree that praise is the point of life. The apparent bleakness of the verse serves as a motive to praise now, and the New Testament shows that the promise of 'for evermore' in verse 18 outlasts the grave.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse asks God to act, and the English hides it. The Hebrew says 'but to Your name give glory,' with an imperative. The psalmists ask the Lord Himself to see to the honour of His name, and they base the request on two attributes that Exodus 34:6 sets side by side, loving devotion and faithfulness. 'Glory' is the Hebrew word kavod, with its root sense of weight or heaviness, so the prayer is that God's real weight will be seen, since the nations' question implies that He weighs nothing.

The word for the idols in verse 4 is atsabbim, from a root usually understood as shaping or fashioning, so the name already carries the meaning 'things made.' The text calls them 'the work of human hands,' a phrase built from the same verb that describes God's action in verse 3, 'He does as He pleases,' and in verse 15, where He is 'Maker' of heaven and earth. It is the play of one root in four places: the Lord does, the idols are things done, their makers do them, and the Lord is the Doer of heaven and earth.

The idols cannot 'speak' in verse 5, and in verse 7 the BSB footnote notes the literal phrase, 'they cannot utter with their throat.' The verb in verse 7 is the verb that Psalm 1:2 uses when the righteous person 'meditates' on the law day and night, a low murmuring. The blessed person mutters Scripture with a voice; the idol cannot manage a murmur.

'Trust' is the root batach, and it appears in verse 8, 'all who trust in them,' and again in verses 9 to 11, 'trust in the LORD.' The same verb is used of the opposite objects. 'Help' and 'shield' are the titles in verses 9 to 11, and they are found together in Psalm 33:20 and are paired with 'the Maker of heaven and earth' in Psalm 124:8.

In verse 12 the Lord 'is mindful' of us. The verb is zakar, remember, which in Hebrew is more an action than a memory, as when God remembered Noah and the waters subsided, Genesis 8:1. In verse 14 'give increase' is the verb yasaf, add, the verb in Rachel's naming of Joseph, Genesis 30:24.

'Silence' in verse 17 is dumah, a word that Psalm 94:17 also uses for the place the psalmist would soon have dwelt if the Lord had not helped him.

The Septuagint counts Psalm 114 and 115 as one psalm, and so reads verse 1 as the ninth verse of its own Psalm 113. Verse 9 follows the Hebrew text, which says 'O Israel,' while the BSB footnote says that many Hebrew manuscripts, the Greek and the Syriac read 'O house of Israel,' matching verses 10 and 12.

typology.type: Idols with eyes that cannot see, verses 5 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The list of senses that the idols lack becomes a list of senses that Jesus gives. Isaiah had foretold the opening of blind eyes and unstopped ears, Isaiah 35:5-6, and Jesus pointed to it as the sign of His work, Matthew 11:5. The crowd's astonishment that He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak, Mark 7:37, answers the mute idols of verse 5. The type falls short, since each healing was a sign and the healed later died; the final restoration comes in the resurrection.

typology.type: Becoming like what we worship, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The principle is that worship moulds the worshipper, and Paul states the redeemed version: those who behold the glory of the Lord are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, 2 Corinthians 3:18. Colossians 1:15 calls the Son the image of the invisible God, so that those who are conformed to Him become what idol-worshippers never could, living images. The correspondence is real, but the difference is that the change here comes by the Spirit and not by mere imitation.

typology.type: The house of Aaron called to trust, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: Aaron's descendants pronounced the Lord's blessing on the people, Numbers 6:22-27, but they were mortal and needed to be replaced, Hebrews 7:23-25. Jesus lifted His hands and blessed the disciples as He ascended, Luke 24:50-53, and He lives forever to intercede, so that those who approach through Him receive what the priestly blessing promised. The pattern is escalated, since the priest here is also the one on whose sacrifice the blessing rests.

typology.type: The living who bless the LORD, verses 17 and 18
typology.fulfillment: The psalm sets the silent dead against the praising living. Jesus answered the same question by saying God is not the God of the dead but of the living, Matthew 22:32, and Paul says the death He died, He died to sin once for all, and the life He lives, He lives to God, Romans 6:10. In Him the 'forevermore' of verse 18 receives its ground. The psalm's picture stops short of resurrection, but the pattern of praise that death cannot silence is the one the gospel finishes.

study.christ:
Psalm 115 leads to Christ most strongly by the question of glory. The psalm opens by turning glory away from people and toward the Lord's name, and Isaiah gives the other side of the same truth: the Lord will not yield His glory to another, Isaiah 42:8 and 48:11. The puzzle the New Testament answers is how Jesus can receive glory and worship without breaking that rule. Paul's hymn in Philippians 2:9-11 says God gave Him the name above all names so that every knee should bow, and the words come from Isaiah 45:23, where the Lord swears that every knee will bow to Him. The verse then ends 'to the glory of God the Father.' The glory goes to the Son and returns to the Father, which shows that He is not 'another' in Isaiah's sense. Jesus Himself prays that the Father would glorify His name, John 12:28, and says that He glorified the Father by finishing the work given to Him, John 17:4.

The second line is the contrast between the dead image and the living Image. Idols have eyes and cannot see. Paul says Christ is the image of God, 2 Corinthians 4:4 and Colossians 1:15, and Jesus tells Philip that anyone who has seen Him has seen the Father, John 14:9. The Image who can see, hear and speak is what the nations' statues pretended to be. The Gospels show Him opening eyes and ears, Mark 7:37, and He is called 'help' in the sense of verses 9 to 11, for since He Himself suffered when tempted He is able to help those who are being tempted, Hebrews 2:18.

Third, the movement from silence to praise. Verse 17 says the dead do not praise the Lord, and verse 18 says the living will, for ever. Jesus entered the silence of the dead and was not left in it, Acts 2:27 and Acts 2:31, so that the praise of the living is no longer interrupted by the grave. This Hallel psalm was part of the Passover liturgy, and Jesus and His disciples sang a hymn before going out to the Mount of Olives, Matthew 26:30. If these words were sung that night, 'Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory' was on lips about to walk to the cross.

The last echo is the blessing that moves both ways. The Lord blesses His people, verse 12, and they bless Him, verse 18. When Jesus blessed His disciples at the ascension, they returned to the temple praising God continually, Luke 24:50-53.

Caution is warranted. The psalm never speaks of a Messiah, and the idol polemic is aimed at statues, not at a person. The links above rest on the New Testament's own words about glory, image and death, and not on a hidden code in the verses.
study.god:
The psalm presents God through three contrasts. Where the nations ask, 'Where is their God?', the answer is that He is in heaven, and that He does as He pleases. The first half of the sentence puts Him beyond the reach of any who would mock or contain Him. The second puts every other power beneath His will. This is the strongest statement of divine freedom in the passage: He needs no defence and cannot be outmanoeuvred.

He is also the God who gives the glory its measure. The grounds on which He is asked to act are His own loving devotion and faithfulness, so that His reputation is no vanity but a matter of His promises being kept in the sight of the world. Ezekiel 36:22-23 develops the same logic. God has bound His name to the people, and He cares about it for their sake and the world's.

The idol section implies a list of attributes by denial. The gods have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear. The living God therefore speaks, sees and hears. The same point is argued in Psalm 94:9, 'He who affixed the ear, can He not hear?' The silent statues are not simply mistaken ideas; they are a standing contrast that makes the character of the real God clear.

He is the God who remembers. The verb is the one used when God remembered Noah, and the promise that follows is concrete: increase, children, blessing on small and great alike. Nothing in the blessing depends on rank, since the sentence has no priority for the great.

He gives as well as keeps. The highest heavens are His, but the earth He has given to humankind, verse 16, echoing the delegated rule of Genesis 1:28. The Lord who does whatever pleases Him has chosen to share the earth with His creatures and to be called their 'help and shield.' His sovereignty does not diminish their agency, and their agency does not rival His.

The tension the psalm holds is between a God enthroned in heaven and a God who is mindful of us. The answer it offers is not an explanation but a posture: the people trust and bless Him, and He blesses them. For worship, the psalm teaches that the first act of praise is to take our own name out of the sentence and to ask that God's name be honoured, then to let that become a joyful, continuing duty as long as we live.

crossReferences.note: Another psalm repeats these four verses almost word for word, with small differences. The agreement shows that the satire of idols was shared worship material, sung in more than one setting, and that Israel considered it the settled answer to the claims of the nations' gods.

Isaiah says of idol makers that their eyes are shut so they cannot see, and that no one stops to think how absurd it is to bow down to a block of wood. It supplies the reasoning behind Psalm 115:8: those who trust blindness become blind.

The idols are compared to scarecrows in a cucumber patch that cannot speak and must be carried because they cannot walk. It matches verse 7's 'feet, but cannot walk' and adds the biting practical point that people have to carry their gods.

The prophet asks what use an idol is, since its maker trusts in his own creation. The word 'trusts' and the picture of the made thing being trusted by its maker both appear in Psalm 115:8, and Habakkuk adds that there is no breath in it.

The question of the nations, 'Why should the nations ask, Where is their God?', is here the cry of a people under attack. It shows what lies behind Psalm 115:2, a real situation of reproach in which God's honour and Israel's suffering were bound together.

God says He will act not for Israel's sake but for His holy name, which they profaned among the nations. It gives the theology behind verse 1: the people are given a new heart and a place not because they deserve it but so the nations will know that He is the LORD.

The same three groups, Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD, are each called to say that His loving devotion endures for ever. It shows that Psalms 115 and 118 are built for the same liturgy, with the congregation answering in turn.

Hezekiah, delivered from death, says that Sheol cannot thank God and that only the living can. It parallels verse 17 and places it in the mouth of a man who was spared, which explains why such a verse is joyful in practice and not morose.

At Lystra, Paul and Barnabas urge the crowd to turn from worthless things to the living God who made heaven and earth and sea. It carries the psalm's contrast of dead idols and the living Maker into the first mission to Gentiles.

Paul says an idol is nothing in the world and that there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. He places Jesus inside the identity of the one Maker, so that the psalm's confession of the sole living God is made to include the Son.

Believers with unveiled faces reflect the glory of the Lord and are transformed into His image. It is the redeemed counterpart of verse 8: resemblance to what one worships is true of the living God as well, and the outcome is life and glory, not blindness.

God exalts Jesus and gives Him the name above all names, with every knee bowing, to the glory of God the Father. Verse 1 refused glory for people, and this passage shows glory given to the Son in a way that does not take it from the Father.

A voice from the throne calls on all God's servants, small and great alike, to praise Him. It repeats the phrase from verse 13 and shows that the blessing on small and great is finally answered by a universal Hallelujah.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 1 says God made humanity in His own image, Genesis 1:26-27, and gave them the earth to rule, Genesis 1:28. Psalm 115 stands in that frame. The earth is given to humankind, verse 16, and the human calling is to bless the Lord who gave it, verse 18. Idolatry is the reversal of the order: people make gods in their own likeness, from the materials of the earth, and then become like what they have made. Paul describes that exchange of the Creator's glory for images in Romans 1:23, and Psalm 106:19-20 uses the same language of the calf at Horeb, 'They exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox.'

The theme runs through every stage of Israel's history. The Ten Commandments forbid making an idol, Exodus 20:4-5, and the gold calf comes within weeks, Exodus 32:2-4. The prophets ridicule idols before and during the exile, and the exile itself is the story of a people who became as deaf and blind as the things they followed. Isaiah 6:10 and Isaiah 44:18 show that the judgment fits the sin. The psalm answers this long history with the invitation to trust the One who is a help and shield, and it calls Israel, Aaron and the God-fearers to do so by name.

With the coming of Christ the answer takes flesh. He is the true Image, 2 Corinthians 4:4, and in Him the nations that served what is by nature not God are turned to the living and true God, Galatians 4:8-9 and 1 Thessalonians 1:9. The call 'keep yourselves from idols,' 1 John 5:21, still closes the New Testament letters, which shows the struggle did not end at the cross. But the people formed by the Spirit are being changed into the image of the Lord, 2 Corinthians 3:18, which is the opposite of the downward slide of verse 8.

The psalm ends with the praise of the living, and the Bible ends the same way. The word 'Hallelujah' occurs in the New Testament only in Revelation 19, where a great multitude cries it out, and a voice calls for praise from small and great alike, Revelation 19:1 and 19:5. In the new creation the curse is gone, God's servants worship Him, they see His face, and His name is on their foreheads, Revelation 22:3-4. The nations' question 'Where is their God?' receives its last answer, because the throne of God and of the Lamb is in the middle of the city.

quiz.q: To whom does the psalmist insist all glory belongs in verse 1?

options.text: To the LORD's name alone, because of His loving devotion and faithfulness.
options.note: The repeated 'not to us' emphatically refuses any human claim to the glory that belongs to God alone.

options.text: To Israel's own military achievements.
options.note: The verse explicitly says 'not to us,' rejecting any claim to glory based on human achievement.

options.text: Equally to Israel and to the LORD.
options.note: The psalm gives no share of glory to Israel; it belongs entirely to God's name.

options.text: To the craftsmen who build the temple.
options.note: The glory is directed to God's name and character, not to any human builders or craftsmen.

quiz.q: According to verses 5-7, what can the idols not do despite having mouths, eyes, ears, and hands?

options.text: Speak, see, hear, smell, feel, or walk.
options.note: This catalogue of inability exposes the total powerlessness of manufactured idols.

options.text: They can do all these things but choose not to.
options.note: The text says they cannot, not that they choose not to; they are simply incapable.

options.text: They can speak but cannot see.
options.note: The text denies all these senses and abilities to the idols, not merely one.

options.text: They can walk but cannot speak.
options.note: The psalm denies walking as well as speaking to these lifeless idols.

quiz.q: What warning does verse 8 give about those who trust in idols?

options.text: They become like them, lifeless and powerless.
options.note: This warns that worship shapes the worshiper into the likeness of the object worshiped.

options.text: They gain the idol's silver and gold as a reward.
options.note: The verse warns of becoming like the idols, not of financial gain.

options.text: They are immediately punished with exile.
options.note: The specific warning given is becoming like the idols, not a statement about exile.

options.text: They become wiser through the experience.
options.note: The warning is the opposite; trusting in idols leads to becoming as lifeless as they are, not gaining wisdom.

quiz.q: Who is called to trust in the LORD in the threefold refrain of verses 9-11?

options.text: Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear the LORD.
options.note: This widening circle includes the nation, its priesthood, and ultimately every reverent worshiper.

options.text: Only the king and his royal court.
options.note: The call extends to Israel, the priesthood, and all who fear the LORD, not merely royalty.

options.text: Only foreign nations, not Israel itself.
options.note: The call is addressed specifically to Israel and the house of Aaron, God's own covenant people, not foreign nations.

options.text: Only the wealthy among God's people.
options.note: The call extends to small and great alike, verse 13, not merely the wealthy.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's pattern of refusing self-glory anticipate Christ?

options.text: Christ's own self-emptying obedience led the Father to exalt Him to the name above every name.
options.note: Philippians 2:9-11 shows this exact pattern, glory refused for self and given wholly to God, fulfilled in Christ's exaltation.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to Christ or the New Testament.
options.note: Philippians 2:9-11 directly parallels this psalm's pattern of humility resulting in exaltation by God.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of Christ's return.
options.note: The psalm's concern is glory rightly directed to God, not a chronological prediction.

options.text: It shows Christ competing with the Father for glory.
options.note: The pattern is the opposite; Christ's humility results in the Father's exaltation of Him, not competition for glory.

questions: The psalm insists that glory belongs not to us but to God's name alone. Where are you tempted to take credit for something that was really God's faithfulness and loving devotion at work?

The idols described have mouths, eyes, and hands but cannot use any of them. What modern 'idols,' things that promise help but cannot truly hear, see, or save, are you tempted to trust instead of God?
Verse 8 warns that we become like what we worship. Looking honestly at your habits and affections this week, what does your life suggest you are actually worshiping?

The threefold call to trust extends from Israel to the priesthood to everyone who fears the LORD, small and great alike. Where do you need to hear this call to trust personally, not just as a general truth about God?
Christ's self-emptying humility led to His exaltation by the Father. Where is God calling you to release your grip on receiving credit or glory, trusting Him to lift you in His own time and way?

translationNotes.note: Idols renders elilim, a Hebrew term whose sound and root evoke worthlessness or nothingness, a built-in mockery of the objects it names.

A variant Hebrew manuscript tradition, along with the Septuagint and Syriac, reads 'O house of Israel' rather than simply 'O Israel,' a minor textual difference that does not affect the psalm's meaning.

The dead do not praise the LORD reflects the Old Testament's typically shadowy portrayal of Sheol, used here to press the urgency of praising God now, while alive, rather than presuming on an unlimited future opportunity.
